```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(gt)
library(here)
library(broom)

here::i_am('seminars/week11-adjustment.qmd')

nhanes <- read_csv(here::here('data', 'mph_nhanes_20241107.csv'), show_col_types = FALSE)

# Recoding, verbatim from chapters/11-adjustment.qmd's own `recode` chunk
# (itself verbatim from Chapter 3): same levels, same labels, same order.
nhanes <- nhanes |>
  mutate(
    gender = factor(gender,
      levels = c(1, 2),
      labels = c('Male', 'Female')),
    eth = factor(eth,
      levels = c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5),
      labels = c('Mexican American', 'Other Hispanic', 'White', 'Black', 'Others')),
    edu = factor(edu,
      levels = c(1, 2, 3),
      labels = c('Less than high school', 'High school graduate', 'Above high school')),
    smoking = factor(smoking,
      levels = c('Never', 'Previous', 'Current')),
    phq.c = factor(phq.c,
      levels = c('0 Normal', '1 Mild symptoms', '2 Possible depression'),
      labels = c('Normal', 'Mild symptoms', 'Possible depression'),
      ordered = TRUE),
    blm.cvd = factor(blm.cvd,
      levels = c(0, 1),
      labels = c('No', 'Yes'))
  )

# Every quantity below is computed the same way chapters/11-adjustment.qmd
# computes it: same variable names, same steps, same function calls.

# sprintf() rather than round(), as in Chapter 7: small slopes otherwise
# print in scientific notation, and dp3 keeps 1.020 from printing as 1.02.
dp5 <- function(x) sprintf('%.5f', x)
dp3 <- function(x) sprintf('%.3f', x)
fmt_p <- function(p) ifelse(p < 0.001, '< 0.001', sprintf('%.3f', p))
# 'p < 0.001' or 'p = 0.070', for p-values inside a sentence
p_txt <- function(p) ifelse(p < 0.001, 'p < 0.001', paste0('p = ', sprintf('%.3f', p)))

# dead_10yr, verbatim from Chapter 7's `dead-10yr` chunk
nhanes <- nhanes |>
  mutate(
    dead_10yr = case_when(
      dth == 1 & fu_month <= 120 ~ 1,
      fu_month >= 120 ~ 0,
      TRUE ~ NA
    )
  )
n_dead <- sum(nhanes$dead_10yr == 1, na.rm = TRUE)
n_alive <- sum(nhanes$dead_10yr == 0, na.rm = TRUE)
n_excluded <- sum(is.na(nhanes$dead_10yr))

# Block 1: chol ~ sed, crude and adjusted, on one sample
chol_adj_complete <- nhanes |>
  filter(!is.na(sed), !is.na(chol), !is.na(age), !is.na(gender), !is.na(edu))
m_adj <- lm(chol ~ sed + age + gender + edu, data = chol_adj_complete)
m_crude <- lm(chol ~ sed, data = chol_adj_complete)
tidy_adj <- tidy(m_adj, conf.int = TRUE)
crude_sed <- tidy(m_crude, conf.int = TRUE) |> filter(term == 'sed')
adj_sed <- tidy_adj |> filter(term == 'sed')

# Week 10's own chol ~ sed slope, on every participant with sed and chol,
# for the 'same participants' slide
sed_complete <- nhanes |> filter(!is.na(sed), !is.na(chol))
w10_sed <- tidy(lm(chol ~ sed, data = sed_complete), conf.int = TRUE) |> filter(term == 'sed')

# met_t, crude and adjusted (the Try it). Same steps as Chapter 7's
# Exercise 1 solution, which now runs on mpa_w so this result isn't spoiled.
met_t_complete <- nhanes |>
  filter(!is.na(met_t), !is.na(chol), !is.na(age), !is.na(gender), !is.na(edu))
crude_met <- tidy(lm(chol ~ met_t, data = met_t_complete), conf.int = TRUE) |> filter(term == 'met_t')
adj_met <- tidy(lm(chol ~ met_t + age + gender + edu, data = met_t_complete), conf.int = TRUE) |>
  filter(term == 'met_t')

# Block 2: chol ~ edu (Chapter 6's model), read as a one-way ANOVA
edu_complete <- nhanes |> filter(!is.na(edu), !is.na(chol))
m_edu <- lm(chol ~ edu, data = edu_complete)
glance_edu <- glance(m_edu)
edu_means <- edu_complete |> group_by(edu) |> summarise(mean_chol = mean(chol), n = n())
adj_aug <- augment(m_adj)

# Block 3: logistic regression, Chapter 7's dead_complete sample
dead_complete <- nhanes |>
  filter(!is.na(dead_10yr), !is.na(sed), !is.na(age), !is.na(gender), !is.na(edu))
m_dead_crude <- glm(dead_10yr ~ sed, data = dead_complete, family = binomial)
m_dead_adj <- glm(dead_10yr ~ sed + age + gender + edu,
  data = dead_complete, family = binomial)
logit_crude_sed <- coef(m_dead_crude)[['sed']]
logit_adj_sed <- coef(m_dead_adj)[['sed']]
or_crude <- tidy(m_dead_crude, exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE) |> filter(term == 'sed')
or_adj <- tidy(m_dead_adj, exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE) |> filter(term == 'sed')

# A straight line through 0/1, drawn on age (checked 2026-09-03: on sed the
# fitted line stays inside 0 to 1 across all plausible values)
lin_bin_data <- nhanes |> filter(!is.na(dead_10yr), !is.na(age))
m_lin_bin <- lm(dead_10yr ~ age, data = lin_bin_data)
lin_min_age <- min(lin_bin_data$age)
lin_at_min <- predict(m_lin_bin, newdata = data.frame(age = lin_min_age))

# vpa_r, crude and adjusted (result only; Chapter 7's Exercise 2 now runs
# on vpa_t so this result isn't spoiled)
vpa_r_dead_complete <- nhanes |>
  filter(!is.na(vpa_r), !is.na(dead_10yr), !is.na(age), !is.na(gender), !is.na(edu))
or_vpa_crude <- tidy(glm(dead_10yr ~ vpa_r, data = vpa_r_dead_complete, family = binomial),
  exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE) |> filter(term == 'vpa_r')
or_vpa_adj <- tidy(glm(dead_10yr ~ vpa_r + age + gender + edu, data = vpa_r_dead_complete,
  family = binomial), exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE) |> filter(term == 'vpa_r')

# Sensitivity analysis, verbatim from Chapter 7's `sensitivity-cvd` chunk
dead_cvd_complete <- dead_complete |> filter(!is.na(blm.cvd))
m_dead_without <- glm(dead_10yr ~ sed + age + gender + edu,
  data = dead_cvd_complete, family = binomial)
m_dead_with <- glm(dead_10yr ~ sed + age + gender + edu + blm.cvd,
  data = dead_cvd_complete, family = binomial)
or_without <- tidy(m_dead_without, exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE) |> filter(term == 'sed')
tidy_with <- tidy(m_dead_with, exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE)
or_with <- tidy_with |> filter(term == 'sed')
or_cvd <- tidy_with |> filter(term == 'blm.cvdYes')

# One three-column result table, built the same way on every slide
result_table <- function(labels, rows, digits) {
  fmt <- if (digits == 5) dp5 else dp3
  tibble(
    Quantity = labels,
    Estimate = fmt(rows$estimate),
    `95% CI` = paste0(fmt(rows$conf.low), ' to ', fmt(rows$conf.high)),
    p = fmt_p(rows$p.value)
  ) |>
    gt()
}

# Paired crude/adjusted intervals on one axis (slides on chol ~ sed, the
# sedentary-time odds ratios, and vpa_r against sed)
forest_plot <- function(df, null, xlab, log_scale = FALSE) {
  df$label <- factor(df$label, levels = rev(df$label))
  p <- ggplot(df, aes(x = estimate, y = label)) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = null, linetype = 'dashed', colour = 'grey40') +
    geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = conf.low, xmax = conf.high), height = 0.2, linewidth = 0.9) +
    geom_point(size = 3) +
    labs(x = xlab, y = NULL) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 18) +
    theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
  if (log_scale) p <- p + scale_x_log10(n.breaks = 5) else p <- p + scale_x_continuous(n.breaks = 4)
  p
}

# Schematic causal diagrams: boxes and arrows, no data
dag_plot <- function(nodes, edges) {
  ggplot() +
    geom_segment(data = edges,
      aes(x = x, y = y, xend = xend, yend = yend),
      arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.3, 'cm'), type = 'closed'), linewidth = 0.8) +
    geom_label(data = nodes, aes(x = x, y = y, label = label),
      size = 6, label.padding = unit(0.5, 'lines')) +
    coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-0.3, 2.3), ylim = c(-0.3, 1.3)) +
    theme_void()
}
dag_nodes <- tibble(x = c(0, 2, 1), y = c(0, 0, 1),
  label = c('Exposure', 'Outcome', 'Confounder'))
dag_edges <- tibble(
  x = c(0.82, 1.18, 0.38), y = c(0.88, 0.88, 0),
  xend = c(0.12, 1.88, 1.6), yend = c(0.16, 0.16, 0))
med_nodes <- tibble(x = c(0, 2, 1), y = c(0, 0, 1),
  label = c('Exposure', 'Outcome', 'Mediator'))
med_edges <- tibble(
  x = c(0.12, 1.18, 0.38), y = c(0.16, 0.88, 0),
  xend = c(0.82, 1.88, 1.6), yend = c(0.88, 0.16, 0))
dag_pair_plot <- function() {
  nodes <- bind_rows(
    dag_nodes |> mutate(panel = 'Confounder'),
    med_nodes |> mutate(panel = 'Mediator'))
  edges <- bind_rows(
    dag_edges |> mutate(panel = 'Confounder'),
    med_edges |> mutate(panel = 'Mediator'))
  dag_plot(nodes, edges) +
    facet_wrap(~ panel, ncol = 1) +
    theme(strip.text = element_blank())
}

# values. Retained from slides_2025/Correlation and Regression AMcI
# 20251114.pptx, slides 40 to 43. The source deck carries the chart only,

# Application: Chan YY, Lim KK, Lim KH, et al. 'Physical activity and
```

## What you have learnt so far {.smaller}

- **Stats, Week 10.** Cholesterol on sedentary time gave a slope of `r sprintf('%.4f', w10_sed$estimate)` mmol/L per hour/day, with a 95% CI spanning zero
  - We left age as a potential confounder
- **Epi, Week 3.** Regression adjustment is one of the main ways to mitigate confounding
- **Epi, Week 4.** Overadjustment bias, mediation, and reverse causation
- **Epi, Week 5.** Residual confounding, information bias, and Bradford Hill

## By the end of this week, you will be able to {.smaller}

1. Specify a multiple linear regression model to account for confounding and interpret the adjusted coefficients
2. Include a categorical explanatory variable, interpret coefficients relative to the reference level, and recognise the equivalence with analysis of variance (ANOVA)
3. Explain why a linear model is unsuitable for a binary response, and why the logistic regression model is a better alternative
4. Interpret an exponentiated coefficient and its confidence interval from a logistic regression

## Block 1: confounding and multiple linear regression {background-image="assets/skyline.jpg" background-size="cover" .divider}

## Was it age all along? {.smaller}

- Last week's slope for cholesterol on sedentary time was small, and its 95% CI spanned zero
- We discussed whether that is convincing evidence of no association
  - Older participants sit for longer
  - Older participants also have higher cholesterol[]{.gap}
- So comparing people who sit more against people who sit less is partly comparing older people against younger ones[]{.gap}
- How can we account for this in regression models?

## Confounding, revisited {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}

- A confounder is a common cause of the exposure (the explanatory variable) and the outcome (the response)
- The arrows are a claim about the world[]{.gap}
- They come from subject knowledge, not from the data (why?)
:::
::: {.column width="55%"}

```{r}
#| label: dag-confounder
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 4
dag_plot(dag_nodes, dag_edges)
```

:::
::::

## A model with several explanatory variables {.smaller}

- Y = α + β~1~X~1~ + β~2~X~2~ + … + β~k~X~k~ + ε
  - Y: the response, e.g., cholesterol in mmol/L
  - X~1~: the exposure, e.g., sedentary time in hours/day
  - X~2~ to X~k~: the other explanatory variables, e.g., age, gender, and education
  - α: the intercept, the mean response when every X is zero
  - β~1~ to β~k~: one coefficient per explanatory variable
  - ε: the error, what the model leaves unexplained[]{.gap}
- The only change from Week 10 is that there is more than one X
- Every assumption from Week 10 carries over unchanged

## What an 'adjustment' means

- β~1~ is the difference in mean response for one unit more of the exposure
- Among people who share the same values of every other variable in the model[]{.gap}
- That is what 'adjusted for age, gender, and education' means
- Some may also describe this as 'holding age, gender, and education constant'

## What an 'adjustment' does not mean {.smaller}

- It does not mean the study held anything constant
  - Nobody was matched, and nobody was restricted
  - The model doesn't actively keep variables unchanged
- It does not mean the estimate is now causal[]{.gap}
- It does commit the model to an assumption:
  - The model estimates one shared slope from everybody at once
  - One extra hour of sitting carries the same association with cholesterol at every age, in both genders, and at each education level (i.e. no effect modification by these)

## Sedentary behaviour and cholesterol, revisited {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: adj-table
#| echo: false
adj_rows <- tidy_adj |> filter(term != '(Intercept)')
tibble(
  Quantity = c(
    'Sedentary time, per hour/day, mmol/L',
    'Age, per year, mmol/L',
    'Women against men, mmol/L',
    "'High school graduate' against 'Less than high school', mmol/L",
    "'Above high school' against 'Less than high school', mmol/L"
  ),
  Estimate = c(dp5(adj_rows$estimate[1:2]), dp3(adj_rows$estimate[3:5])),
  `95% CI` = c(
    paste0(dp5(adj_rows$conf.low[1:2]), ' to ', dp5(adj_rows$conf.high[1:2])),
    paste0(dp3(adj_rows$conf.low[3:5]), ' to ', dp3(adj_rows$conf.high[3:5]))
  ),
  p = fmt_p(adj_rows$p.value)
) |>
  gt()
```

- `r format(nobs(m_adj), big.mark = ',')` participants with sedentary time, cholesterol, age, gender, and education recorded[]{.gap}
- After adjustment for age, gender, and education, each additional hour/day of sedentary time was associated with `r dp5(abs(adj_sed$estimate))` mmol/L lower cholesterol (95% CI `r dp5(abs(adj_sed$conf.high))` to `r dp5(abs(adj_sed$conf.low))` mmol/L lower, p = `r dp3(adj_sed$p.value)`)
- How should we interpret the rows for age, gender, and education?

## Crude and adjusted, side by side {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: crude-adj-table
#| echo: false
result_table(
  c('Crude, per hour/day, mmol/L', 'Adjusted for age, gender, and education, per hour/day, mmol/L'),
  bind_rows(crude_sed, adj_sed), digits = 5)
```

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="40%"}

- The crude 95% CI includes zero, and the adjusted one doesn't
- The estimate moved further from zero
- The CI did not narrow
- After adjustment for age, gender, and education, more sedentary time is associated with slightly lower cholesterol
:::
::: {.column width="60%"}

```{r}
#| label: crude-adj-forest
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3.2
forest_plot(
  bind_rows(crude_sed, adj_sed) |> mutate(label = c('Crude', 'Adjusted')),
  null = 0, xlab = 'mmol/L per hour/day of sedentary time')
```

:::
::::

## Both models, the same participants {.smaller}

- Requiring age, gender, and education to be recorded drops some participants because of missing data
- So the crude model is refitted on the participants the adjusted model could use[]{.gap}
- Otherwise any movement between the two could be the adjustment, or the change of sample
- Nothing in the output would say which[]{.gap}
- This is why the crude slope here is `r dp5(crude_sed$estimate)` mmol/L per hour/day, not Week 10's `r sprintf('%.4f', w10_sed$estimate)`

## Reading the change

- Look at the estimate first
- The adjusted slope is about `r round(adj_sed$estimate / crude_sed$estimate, 1)` times the size of the crude one
- Adjusting for age, gender, and education pulls the association further from zero
- The crude model was understating it, assuming we are sure the adjusted variables are true confounders

## Try it: what did adjustment do here? {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: tryit-met-table
#| echo: false
result_table(
  c('Total physical activity, crude, per MET-hour/day, mmol/L',
    'Total physical activity, adjusted for age, gender, and education, per MET-hour/day, mmol/L'),
  bind_rows(crude_met, adj_met), digits = 5)
```

- What has changed between the two rows?
- Describe the two results in two sentences
- Five minutes, in pairs

## Try it: the answer {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: answer-met-table
#| echo: false
result_table(
  c('Total physical activity, crude, per MET-hour/day, mmol/L',
    'Total physical activity, adjusted for age, gender, and education, per MET-hour/day, mmol/L'),
  bind_rows(crude_met, adj_met), digits = 5)
```

- The estimate changed sign
  - Crude: each additional MET-hour/day of total physical activity was associated with `r dp5(abs(crude_met$estimate))` mmol/L lower cholesterol (95% CI `r dp5(abs(crude_met$conf.low))` lower to `r dp5(crude_met$conf.high)` higher, p = `r dp3(crude_met$p.value)`)
  - Adjusted for age, gender, and education: each additional MET-hour/day was associated with `r dp5(adj_met$estimate)` mmol/L higher cholesterol (95% CI `r dp5(adj_met$conf.low)` to `r dp5(adj_met$conf.high)`, `r p_txt(adj_met$p.value)`)[]{.gap}
- The adjusted row is the better estimate of the association
  - The crude row compares active people against inactive people who also differ in age and gender
- Adjustment still doesn't guarantee a causal estimate
  - It is closer to one than the crude estimate, since age, gender, and education are likely confounders

## Table 2 fallacy {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: table2-adj-table
#| echo: false
tibble(
  Quantity = c(
    'Sedentary time, per hour/day, mmol/L',
    'Age, per year, mmol/L',
    'Women against men, mmol/L',
    "'High school graduate' against 'Less than high school', mmol/L",
    "'Above high school' against 'Less than high school', mmol/L"
  ),
  Estimate = c(dp5(adj_rows$estimate[1:2]), dp3(adj_rows$estimate[3:5])),
  `95% CI` = c(
    paste0(dp5(adj_rows$conf.low[1:2]), ' to ', dp5(adj_rows$conf.high[1:2])),
    paste0(dp3(adj_rows$conf.low[3:5]), ' to ', dp3(adj_rows$conf.high[3:5]))
  ),
  p = fmt_p(adj_rows$p.value)
) |>
  gt() |>
  tab_options(data_row.padding = px(3))
```

- Suppose sitting lies on the pathway from age to cholesterol
  - Part of age's association then runs through sitting
  - Age's adjusted coefficient captures only the rest[]{.gap}
  - The overadjustment bias from Epi Week 4
- Reading every coefficient as if they're causal is the **Table 2 fallacy**
  - [Westreich and Greenland (2013)](https://doi.org/10.1093/aje/kws412), *American Journal of Epidemiology*
- The confounders' own coefficients are usually not presented: overadjustment, or their own confounders, can bias them

## The difference between a confounder and a mediator {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="58%"}

- A confounder is a common cause of the exposure and the outcome
  - Adjusting for it removes bias
- A mediator lies on the path between them
  - Adjusting for it removes part of the association we set out to estimate
  - This is overadjustment bias, from Week 4[]{.gap}
:::
::: {.column width="42%"}

```{r}
#| label: dag-pair
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 5
dag_pair_plot()
```

:::
::::

## The data cannot tell them apart

- If a variable is associated with both exposure and outcome
  - It can be a confounder
  - But also a mediator, and a collider[]{.gap}
- Confounder or mediator is a causal judgement, made before the analysis
  - It rests on subject knowledge and on the study design
- No statistical test or software makes it for us

## Try it: adjust, or leave it out? {.smaller}

| | Exposure | Outcome | Third variable |
|--|----------|---------|----------------|
| A | Sedentary time | Cholesterol | Age |
| B | Salt intake | Stroke | Blood pressure |
| C | Alcohol intake | Lung cancer | Smoking |
| D | Sedentary time | Death | Baseline cardiovascular disease |

- For each row:
  - Is the third variable most plausibly a confounder or a mediator?
  - What would adjusting for it do to the estimate?
- Three to five minutes, in pairs

## Try it: the answer {.smaller}

| | Exposure | Outcome | Third variable | Role | Adjusting for it |
|--|----------|---------|----------------|------|------------------|
| A | Sedentary time | Cholesterol | Age | Confounder | Reduces confounding bias |
| B | Salt intake | Stroke | Blood pressure | Mediator | Introduces overadjustment bias |
| C | Alcohol intake | Lung cancer | Smoking | Confounder or prognostic factor | Reduces confounding bias or improves precision |
| D | Sedentary time | Death | Baseline cardiovascular disease | Cannot be settled from these data | Block 3 returns to it |

## This week's methodological anchor {.smaller}

- Which variables to adjust for depends on causal assumptions, not on patterns in the data[]{.gap}
- Confounders should usually be adjusted for
- Mediators should not be, when the question is about the total association
- Colliders, common effects of the exposure and the outcome, should not be either[]{.gap}
- Where the causal role is unclear, fit the model under each plausible role and report them all
- [Ho (2025)](https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjmed-2023-000816), *BMJ Medicine*: 'Regression adjustment for causal inference'
- Judging whether a sentence says what the numbers support is where half the assessment marks are

## Block 2: Regression and ANOVA {background-image="assets/skyline.jpg" background-size="cover" .divider}

## One categorical variable: one-way ANOVA {.smaller}

- Analysis of variance (ANOVA) asks whether the mean response is equal across three or more groups
- It answers with the F statistic:
  - F = mean square between groups / mean square within groups
    - Mean square between = sum of squares between groups / (k − 1), for k groups
    - Mean square within = sum of squares within groups / (n − k), for n participants
  - Intuitively, this is the ratio of between-group variation to within-group variation
  - A large F statistic means the group means sit further apart than the spread inside the groups accounts for
- A regression on one categorical explanatory variable with three or more levels asks the same question
  - The F statistic from Week 10 is the same as the ANOVA F statistic

## Between-group and within-group variation {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="40%"}

- Between-group variation: how far the group means sit from each other
- Within-group variation: how far each participant sits from their own group's mean[]{.gap}
- Top: the means are far apart and each group is tight, so F is large
- Bottom: the means are close and each group is spread out, so F is small
:::
::: {.column width="60%"}

```{r}
#| label: anova-illustration
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 5
set.seed(11)
anova_demo <- bind_rows(
  tibble(panel = 'Large F', group = rep(c('A', 'B', 'C'), each = 30),
    y = rnorm(90, mean = rep(c(3, 6, 9), each = 30), sd = 0.7)),
  tibble(panel = 'Small F', group = rep(c('A', 'B', 'C'), each = 30),
    y = rnorm(90, mean = rep(c(5.6, 6, 6.4), each = 30), sd = 2.2))
)
anova_means <- anova_demo |> group_by(panel, group) |> summarise(y = mean(y), .groups = 'drop')
ggplot(anova_demo, aes(x = group, y = y)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, height = 0, alpha = 0.5, colour = 'grey40') +
  geom_errorbar(data = anova_means, aes(ymin = y, ymax = y), width = 0.5,
    linewidth = 1.2, colour = '#00213B') +
  facet_wrap(~ panel, ncol = 1) +
  labs(x = 'Group', y = 'Response') +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 16) +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank(), panel.grid = element_blank(),
    strip.text = element_text(face = 'bold', size = 16))
```

:::
::::

## Does mean cholesterol differ by education? {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: edu-means
#| echo: false
edu_means |>
  transmute(
    Education = as.character(edu),
    `Participants` = format(n, big.mark = ','),
    `Mean cholesterol, mmol/L` = dp3(mean_chol)
  ) |>
  gt()
```

- H0: mean cholesterol is the same in all three education groups
- H1: at least one group's mean differs[]{.gap}
- F = `r dp3(glance_edu$statistic)` on `r glance_edu$df` and `r format(glance_edu$df.residual, big.mark = ',')` degrees of freedom, p = `r dp3(glance_edu$p.value)`
- No evidence of a difference in mean cholesterol between the three groups
- The same model as Week 10, read as one question across all three groups

## Try it: how far apart are the groups?

```{r}
#| label: tryit-edu-means
#| echo: false
edu_means |>
  transmute(
    Education = as.character(edu),
    `Mean cholesterol, mmol/L` = dp3(mean_chol)
  ) |>
  gt()
```

- Which two groups differ most, and by how much, in mmol/L?
- Is that consistent with F = `r dp3(glance_edu$statistic)`?
- Three minutes

## Try it: the answer

```{r}
#| label: answer-edu-means
#| echo: false
edu_means |>
  transmute(
    Education = as.character(edu),
    `Mean cholesterol, mmol/L` = dp3(mean_chol)
  ) |>
  gt()
```

- 'Less than high school' and 'High school graduate' differ most: `r dp3(max(edu_means$mean_chol) - min(edu_means$mean_chol))` mmol/L
- Tiny, set against how much cholesterol varies inside each group[]{.gap}
- So the between-group mean square is small next to the within-group one, and F is small

## Why not compare the groups in pairs?

- Sometimes we want to know whether a categorical variable matters, instead of which group has the higher or lower response
- Also, three groups give three pairwise comparisons, which makes at least one Type I error more likely[]{.gap}
- Where pairwise comparisons are wanted afterwards, each CI has to be widened to keep the whole set at 95%
  - Bonferroni is the simplest way of doing this

## Diagnostics, several explanatory variables

- The four assumptions from Week 10 are unchanged
  - Linearity, constant variance, normally distributed residuals, independence
- The same two plots check them[]{.gap}
- The fitted value now combines several explanatory variables
- So the horizontal axis of the residual plot is no longer any one variable

## Adjusted model: residuals against fitted {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="38%"}

- The same picture as Week 10
- An even band around zero for most of the range
- No visible trend, and the spread looks constant[]{.gap}
- A small group with unusually high cholesterol sits well above the band
:::
::: {.column width="62%"}

```{r}
#| label: diag-resid
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 5
ggplot(adj_aug, aes(x = .fitted, y = .resid)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.1) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
  labs(x = 'Fitted value (mmol/L)', y = 'Residual (mmol/L)')
```

:::
::::

## Adjusted model: the QQ plot {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="38%"}

- The middle of the distribution sits close to the line
- The same high-cholesterol participants pull the upper tail away from it[]{.gap}
- With `r format(nobs(m_adj), big.mark = ',')` participants, the estimates hold up despite it
:::
::: {.column width="62%"}

```{r}
#| label: diag-qq
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 5
ggplot(adj_aug, aes(sample = .std.resid)) +
  stat_qq() +
  stat_qq_line() +
  labs(x = 'Theoretical quantiles', y = 'Standardised residuals')
```

:::
::::

## The response has always been a measurement

- Everything so far has changed the right-hand side of the model
  - More explanatory variables, better questions[]{.gap}
- The response has been cholesterol every time, a measurement in mmol/L
- Almost every outcome in the epidemiology half is not a measurement
  - Died or survived, improved or not, diagnosed or not

## Block 3: when the response is binary {background-image="assets/skyline.jpg" background-size="cover" .divider}

## Most epidemiology outcomes are binary {.smaller}

- Improvement in the streptomycin trial
- Incidence of a disease[]{.gap}
- Death
- None of these is a measurement
- The linear regression models we used need a continuous response
- But what if we still fit a binary variable using linear regression?

## The outcome: died within ten years {.smaller}

- The survey records whether each participant died during follow-up, and how long they were followed
- To create a binary variable, participants are categorised into three groups:
  - Died within 120 months: an event, coded 1
  - Known to be alive at 120 months, whether or not they died later: coded 0
  - Alive, but followed for less than 120 months: cannot be classified either way, so excluded

## What that costs, and what the models use {.smaller}

| Group | Participants |
|-------|-------------:|
| Died within ten years | `r format(n_dead, big.mark = ',')` |
| Known alive at ten years | `r format(n_alive, big.mark = ',')` |
| Excluded: follow-up ended too early | `r format(n_excluded, big.mark = ',')` |

- The models in this block run on a smaller set again: `r format(nrow(dead_complete), big.mark = ',')` participants, `r format(sum(dead_complete$dead_10yr), big.mark = ',')` events
  - Every explanatory variable has to be recorded
- A fixed window ignores the timing of death
  - Survival analysis keeps that, and the excluded participants: Advanced Statistics
- The number of events limits how many explanatory variables the model can carry
  - So the adjustment set stays at three

## A straight line through zeros and ones {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="38%"}

- Ten-year mortality against age, with a straight line fitted
- At age `r lin_min_age`, the youngest age in the sample, the line gives `r sprintf('%.3f', lin_at_min)`
  - A value below zero is not a probability[]{.gap}
- The line also describes the binary response variable poorly
:::
::: {.column width="62%"}

```{r}
#| label: linear-on-binary
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 5
ggplot(lin_bin_data, aes(x = age, y = dead_10yr)) +
  geom_jitter(height = 0.04, width = 0, alpha = 0.03) +
  geom_abline(intercept = coef(m_lin_bin)[[1]], slope = coef(m_lin_bin)[[2]],
    colour = '#00213B', linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = c(0, 1), linetype = 'dashed', colour = 'grey40') +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = c(0, 0.5, 1)) +
  labs(x = 'Age (years)', y = 'Died within ten years (0 = no, 1 = yes)')
```

:::
::::

## The fix: model the log odds

- From Week 2: odds = number with the outcome / number without it
- An odds ratio is one group's odds divided by another's[]{.gap}
- A probability is bounded between zero and one, which is what broke the straight line
- The log of the odds runs from minus infinity to plus infinity
  - That is the range a straight line needs[]{.gap}
- So the model works on the log odds, with the same right-hand side as Block 1

## The logistic regression model {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}

$$P(Y = 1) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-(\alpha + \beta_1 X_1 + \dots + \beta_k X_k)}}$$

- Y is the binary response, e.g., died within ten years
  - X~1~ to X~k~: the explanatory variables, as in Block 1
  - α and β~1~ to β~k~: on the log-odds scale[]{.gap}
- Whatever the exponent's value, P(Y = 1) stays between 0 and 1
- Rearranged: log(odds) = α + β~1~X~1~ + … + β~k~X~k~
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}

```{r}
#| label: sigmoid
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 4.5
tibble(lp = seq(-6, 6, by = 0.05)) |>
  mutate(prob = plogis(lp)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = lp, y = prob)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = c(0, 1), linetype = 'dashed', colour = 'grey40') +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2, colour = '#00213B') +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = c(0, 0.5, 1)) +
  labs(x = 'Log odds: α + β₁X₁ + … (any value)', y = 'Probability (0 to 1)') +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 16)
```

:::
::::

## How to estimate the coefficients {.smaller}

- Linear regression used least squares, and its CIs and p-values rest on Week 10's assumptions
- A binary response breaks them:
  - At any fitted value, a residual can take only two values, so residuals cannot be normal
  - The spread is p(1 − p), largest near 0.5, so it is not constant
  - The fitted line can leave 0 to 1, as two slides back[]{.gap}
- A larger sample does not fix any of these
- Maximum likelihood instead chooses the coefficients that make the observed 0s and 1s most probable
- Where linear regression's assumptions hold, least squares and maximum likelihood give the same answer

## What the software gives back

- The crude model of ten-year mortality on sedentary time returns a coefficient of `r sprintf('%.4f', logit_crude_sed)` per hour/day
- That number is on the log-odds scale[]{.gap}
- Log-odds difference is usually not reported because it doesn't have epidemiological meaning
- The reportable version needs one more step

## Why exponentiating gives an odds ratio {.smaller}

- Compare X~1~ = x with X~1~ = x + 1, every other X unchanged

$$\begin{aligned}
\log(\text{odds}_{x+1}) &= \alpha + \beta_1 (x + 1) + \beta_2 X_2 + \dots \\
\log(\text{odds}_{x}) &= \alpha + \beta_1 x + \beta_2 X_2 + \dots \\
\log(\text{odds}_{x+1}) - \log(\text{odds}_{x}) &= \beta_1
\end{aligned}$$

- Every other term is the same on both lines, so it cancels
- A difference of logs is the log of a ratio

$$\log\left(\frac{\text{odds}_{x+1}}{\text{odds}_{x}}\right) = \log(\text{OR}) = \beta_1 \quad\text{so}\quad \text{OR} = e^{\beta_1}$$

## Exponentiate it: an odds ratio

- e^`r sprintf('%.4f', logit_crude_sed)`^ = `r dp3(exp(logit_crude_sed))`[]{.gap}
- The odds ratio from Epi Week 2
- The principle of adjustment also works for logistic regression

## Sitting and ten-year mortality {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: or-table
#| echo: false
result_table(
  c('Crude odds ratio, per hour/day', 'Odds ratio adjusted for age, gender, and education, per hour/day'),
  bind_rows(or_crude, or_adj), digits = 3)
```

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}

- Crude: each additional hour/day of sedentary time was associated with `r sprintf('%.1f', (or_crude$estimate - 1) * 100)`% higher odds of dying within ten years (OR `r dp3(or_crude$estimate)`, 95% CI `r dp3(or_crude$conf.low)` to `r dp3(or_crude$conf.high)`, `r p_txt(or_crude$p.value)`)[]{.gap}
- Both 95% CIs sit entirely above 1
- The adjusted estimate is the smaller
- Part of the crude association was age
  - Older participants both sit more and are more likely to die within ten years
:::
::: {.column width="55%"}

```{r}
#| label: or-forest
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 3.2
forest_plot(
  bind_rows(or_crude, or_adj) |> mutate(label = c('Crude', 'Adjusted')),
  null = 1, xlab = 'Odds ratio (log scale)', log_scale = TRUE)
```

:::
::::

## An odds ratio as a percentage change

- An odds ratio above 1: (OR − 1) × 100% higher odds
  - e.g., `r dp3(or_crude$estimate)` is `r sprintf('%.1f', (or_crude$estimate - 1) * 100)`% higher odds per hour/day
- An odds ratio below 1: (1 − OR) × 100% lower odds
  - e.g., 0.80 is 20% lower odds[]{.gap}
- Convert both CI limits the same way: `r sprintf('%.1f', (or_crude$conf.low - 1) * 100)`% to `r sprintf('%.1f', (or_crude$conf.high - 1) * 100)`% higher
- It is a change in the odds, not in the risk

## The null value is 1, not 0

- No association on the odds ratio scale is an odds ratio of 1
- The same point Week 9 made for the risk ratio and the odds ratio from a 2x2 table[]{.gap}
- A 95% CI that excludes 1 is the ratio-scale version of one that excludes zero
- Both 95% CIs on the previous slide exclude 1

## Try it: coefficient to odds ratio

- The adjusted model's coefficient for sedentary time is `r sprintf('%.5f', logit_adj_sed)` on the log-odds scale, per hour/day[]{.gap}
- Turn it into an odds ratio for one extra hour a day, and describe it in one or two sentences, with the 95% CI and p from the mortality table
- Bonus question: Give the odds ratio for five extra hours a day
- Five minutes

## Try it: the answer {.smaller}

- e^`r sprintf('%.5f', logit_adj_sed)`^ = `r dp3(exp(logit_adj_sed))`, the adjusted odds ratio in the mortality table
- After adjustment for age, gender, and education, each additional hour/day of sedentary time was associated with `r sprintf('%.1f', (or_adj$estimate - 1) * 100)`% higher odds of dying within ten years (OR `r dp3(or_adj$estimate)`, 95% CI `r dp3(or_adj$conf.low)` to `r dp3(or_adj$conf.high)`, `r p_txt(or_adj$p.value)`)[]{.gap}
- Bonus, five hours: `r dp3(exp(logit_adj_sed))`^5^ ≈ `r sprintf('%.2f', exp(5 * logit_adj_sed))`, about `r round((exp(5 * logit_adj_sed) - 1) * 100)`% higher odds
  - Not `r dp3(exp(logit_adj_sed))` × 5[]{.gap}
- The model is additive on the log-odds scale
- Exponentiating turns adding into multiplying
- So odds ratios multiply across units

## When adjustment moves the answer a lot {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: vpa-table
#| echo: false
result_table(
  c('Vigorous activity outside work, crude odds ratio, per hour/day',
    'Vigorous activity outside work, adjusted odds ratio, per hour/day'),
  bind_rows(or_vpa_crude, or_vpa_adj), digits = 3)
```

- Crude: each additional hour/day of vigorous activity outside work was associated with `r round((1 - or_vpa_crude$estimate) * 100)`% lower odds of dying within ten years (OR `r dp3(or_vpa_crude$estimate)`, 95% CI `r dp3(or_vpa_crude$conf.low)` to `r dp3(or_vpa_crude$conf.high)`, `r p_txt(or_vpa_crude$p.value)`)
- Adjusted for age, gender, and education: `r round((1 - or_vpa_adj$estimate) * 100)`% lower odds (OR `r dp3(or_vpa_adj$estimate)`, 95% CI `r dp3(or_vpa_adj$conf.low)` to `r dp3(or_vpa_adj$conf.high)`, `r p_txt(or_vpa_adj$p.value)`)

## How far adjustment moved it {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}

- Still a substantial association, but far smaller
  - Most of the crude association was age[]{.gap}
- Sedentary time, for comparison, moved far less on this scale
- The lab's Exercise 2 repeats this on vigorous activity overall
:::
::: {.column width="55%"}

```{r}
#| label: vpa-forest
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 3.6
forest_plot(
  bind_rows(or_vpa_crude, or_vpa_adj, or_crude, or_adj) |>
    mutate(label = c('Vigorous activity, crude', 'Vigorous activity, adjusted',
      'Sedentary time, crude', 'Sedentary time, adjusted')),
  null = 1, xlab = 'Odds ratio (log scale)', log_scale = TRUE)
```

:::
::::

## A harder case: baseline heart disease

- Existing heart disease could make someone both less active and more likely to die
  - A confounder, worth adjusting for[]{.gap}
- Or sitting could contribute to heart disease, which then contributes to death
  - A mediator, and adjusting for it removes part of what we set out to estimate[]{.gap}
- Both are biologically plausible

## Why the data cannot decide

- Sedentary time and baseline cardiovascular disease were recorded at the same study visit
- Nothing in the data establishes which came first[]{.gap}
- This is not a gap in the analysis, and more data would not close it
- It is a limitation of the lack of temporality in the measurements

## What a sensitivity analysis is

- An analysis can rest on an assumption we are not certain of
- A sensitivity analysis fits the model under each competing assumption and reports them all[]{.gap}
- It cannot say which assumption is right
- It is not a test with a verdict
- It says whether the conclusion depends on the assumption at all

## Sensitivity analysis: the two models {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: sensitivity-table
#| echo: false
result_table(
  c('Without baseline cardiovascular disease (assumes a mediator), odds ratio per hour/day',
    'With baseline cardiovascular disease (assumes a confounder), odds ratio per hour/day'),
  bind_rows(or_without, or_with), digits = 3)
```

- Baseline cardiovascular disease is itself strongly associated with dying within ten years
  - Odds ratio `r dp3(or_cvd$estimate)` (95% CI `r dp3(or_cvd$conf.low)` to `r dp3(or_cvd$conf.high)`, p < 0.001)[]{.gap}
- Without it: OR `r dp3(or_without$estimate)` per hour/day of sedentary time (95% CI `r dp3(or_without$conf.low)` to `r dp3(or_without$conf.high)`, `r p_txt(or_without$p.value)`)
- With it: OR `r dp3(or_with$estimate)` (95% CI `r dp3(or_with$conf.low)` to `r dp3(or_with$conf.high)`, `r p_txt(or_with$p.value)`)[]{.gap}
- Adjusting for it changes almost nothing about the sedentary time estimate
- Whether baseline cardiovascular disease is a confounder or a mediator, the conclusion about sedentary time and death is the same

## What adjustment can and cannot fix

- Regression adjustment is a powerful tool, and one of the most used statistical tools to mitigate confounding, but it cannot fix:
  - Confounders that were measured badly (information bias, leading to residual confounding)
  - Confounders that were never measured at all (unmeasured confounding)
  - Participants missing from the analysis (selection bias)
  - Adjusting for the wrong variable (overadjustment bias)[]{.gap}

## Application {background-image="assets/skyline.jpg" background-size="cover" .divider}

## Crude, adjusted, and no interpretation {.smaller}

- Overweight or obesity in Malaysian men, by physical activity level, with selected other rows

| Comparison | Crude OR (95% CI) | Adjusted OR (95% CI) |
|------------------|-------------|-------------|
| Physical activity: low against high | 1.28 (1.10 to 1.49) | 1.06 (0.91 to 1.24) |
| Physical activity: moderate against high | 1.34 (1.18 to 1.51) | 1.14 (1.01 to 1.30) |
| Age 40 to 49 against 18 to 29 | 1.98 (1.65 to 2.37) | 1.44 (1.14 to 1.81) |
| Age 60 or over against 18 to 29 | 1.32 (1.10 to 1.58) | 0.74 (0.56 to 0.98) |
| Tertiary education against none | 2.49 (1.81 to 3.44) | 1.67 (1.20 to 2.33) |

- Adjusted for age, ethnicity, area, marital status, education, income, sitting time, diabetes, hypertension, and high cholesterol[]{.gap}
- In pairs, ten minutes:
  - Interpret the adjusted odds ratio for moderate against high activity, in context, and state what it is adjusted for
  - Pick any other coefficients: could the same sentence honestly be written about it?
- [Chan et al. (2017)](https://doi.org/10.1186/s12889-017-4772-z), *BMC Public Health*, Table 3, men only

## The sentences, and what the authors wrote {.smaller}

| Comparison | Crude OR (95% CI) | Adjusted OR (95% CI) |
|------------------|-------------|-------------|
| Physical activity: moderate against high | 1.34 (1.18 to 1.51) | 1.14 (1.01 to 1.30) |

- Men with moderate activity had 1.14 times the odds of overweight or obesity of men with high activity (95% CI 1.01 to 1.30), after adjustment for the variables listed
- The authors: 'A low level of PA was associated with the risk of overweight/obesity (Adjusted OR = 1.14; 95% CI: 1.01–1.30) compared to a high level of PA among men'
  - 1.14 is the moderate row, not the low row
  - An odds ratio is not a risk[]{.gap}
- Diabetes, hypertension, and high cholesterol may follow from overweight, not precede it
  - Adjusting for them is a judgement the table does not justify

## The other coefficients {.smaller}

- All coefficients are mutually adjusted
- But the adjustment set was chosen for physical activity, not for age or education
  - So the same sentence cannot honestly be written about the other rows: the Table 2 fallacy[]{.gap}
- The authors: 'Among the socio-demographic variables, age, ethnicity and educational level were significantly associated with being overweight/obese'
- [Chan et al. (2017)](https://doi.org/10.1186/s12889-017-4772-z), *BMC Public Health*, CC BY 4.0, Table 3, men only

## A cautionary tale {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="38%"}

- Year trend for student activity in Scottish further education
- A statistician was asked to predict the next point in this sequence
- They fitted a straight line, and predicted the red point: about `r format(round(tale_pred_2000, -1), big.mark = ',')`
- The actual value was the green point: about `r format(tale_actual_2000, big.mark = ',')`[]{.gap}
- The data had levelled off, and a straight line cannot

:::
::: {.column width="62%"}

```{r}
#| label: cautionary-tale
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 5
ggplot(tale, aes(x = year, y = activity)) +
  geom_abline(intercept = coef(m_tale)[[1]], slope = coef(m_tale)[[2]],
    colour = '#00213B', linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  annotate('point', x = 2000, y = tale_pred_2000, colour = 'red', size = 4) +
  annotate('point', x = 2000, y = tale_actual_2000, colour = 'forestgreen', size = 4) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1993:2000) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(4000, 8000)) +
  labs(x = 'Year', y = 'Student activity (thousand hours)') +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 16)
```

:::
::::

## Always look at the data first

- Plot before modelling
  - Week 7's descriptive statistics
  - Week 10's scatterplot
  - This week's diagnostics[]{.gap}
- A model always returns a number, whatever shape the data are

## Where this goes next {.smaller}

- Not covered here:
  - Model fit statistics: deviance and pseudo R squared
  - Diagnostics specific to logistic regression
  - Interaction, prediction, and discrimination[]{.gap}
- Picked up by Advanced Statistics:
  - Model building, and why stepwise selection is a poor way to do it
  - Explanation against prediction, and multicollinearity
  - Formal mediation analysis
  - Survival analysis, for the follow-up time this session set aside
  - Logistic regression in full

## Key points, and what the lab does {.smaller}

- A crude association can mislead, and adjustment is how a regression addresses it
- An adjusted coefficient is an association among people alike in everything else the model holds
- Beware the Table 2 fallacy when interpreting the other variables' coefficients[]{.gap}
- Exponentiate a logistic regression coefficient to derive an odds ratio, with the null at 1
- Sensitivity analysis is a tool to help when you want to examine if an assumption is important[]{.gap}
- The lab derives the ten-year mortality outcome, fits both model types, and builds the crude-and-adjusted and sensitivity tables
